---

# Locality Guide: New York City, New York (1700s Colonial Period)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** New York City traces to the Dutch colony of New Amsterdam, founded 1626 on Manhattan Island. The English seized it in 1664, renaming it New York. By 1700 it was organized as New York County under British colonial rule.
- **County seat / administrative center:** New York (Manhattan)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Province of New York (British colonial), under the British Crown
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the population tool for this query. Estimates drawn from Wikipedia place the city at roughly 5,000 in 1700, growing to approximately 25,000 by 1790 (the first federal census), making it one of the largest cities in colonial North America.
- **Economy:** Major commercial seaport; fur trade, mercantile shipping, artisan crafts, shipbuilding, and retail trade. A significant enslaved-labor economy operated throughout the period.
- **Ethnic composition:** The 1700s population was a mix of Dutch families (descendants of the pre-1664 settlers), English newcomers, Huguenot (French Protestant) refugees, a Jewish community of Sephardic origin, African enslaved persons and some free Black residents, and smaller German and Scottish contingents.
- **Religious denominations:** Dutch Reformed (oldest continuous congregation, 1628), Anglican/Church of England (Trinity Church, founded 1698), Presbyterian (First Presbyterian, 1716), Lutheran, Quaker (Friends), Jewish (Shearith Israel, the oldest US synagogue, 1730 building), and French Huguenot congregations.
- **Key historical events:** Leisler's Rebellion 1689-1691 (political upheaval that split the Dutch and English populations); Queen Anne's War 1702-1713; King George's War 1744-1748; French and Indian War 1754-1763; British occupation of New York City throughout the entire Revolutionary War (1776-1783), during which many Loyalist families fled and patriot records were disrupted.

## Boundary changes

- The city in the 1700s was confined to the southern tip of Manhattan (present-day lower Manhattan). New York County was coextensive with Manhattan throughout this period.
- The five-borough consolidation that created the modern City of New York did not occur until 1898 — Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx, and Staten Island were separate jurisdictions during the colonial period.
- Kings County (Brooklyn), Queens County, Richmond County (Staten Island), and Westchester County (which then included much of the Bronx) were all neighboring jurisdictions with their own separate record series. Families living near the ferry crossings to Brooklyn or the upper Manhattan border generated records in multiple counties.
- During the Revolutionary War (1776-1783), British military occupation disrupted record-keeping. Some records created under the Crown may be held in British repositories (e.g., The National Archives, Kew, London).

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** There was no statewide civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths in New York during the 1700s. New York State did not require statewide vital registration until 1880 (and compliance was poor until the early 1900s). The FamilySearch Wiki Vital Records page returned only generic content for this query; the FamilySearch Wiki does not state a specific registration date for the city level during the colonial period. The FamilySearch collection "New York, County Marriages, 1847-1849; 1907-1936" (Collection ID 1920153) shows the earliest indexed marriage records begin in 1847 — well after the colonial period.
- **What exists for the 1700s:** No civil vital registration. All birth, marriage, and death recording was done by individual churches.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers are the essential substitute — see Church Records below. Probate records (wills, inventories) establish family members and death dates. Newspaper notices in the New York Gazette (founded 1725) announced marriages and deaths for prominent families.

### Church records

This is the single most important record category for New York City in the 1700s. No civil vital registration existed; churches were the only systematic recorders of baptisms, marriages, and burials.

- **Denominations present:** Dutch Reformed (registers beginning 1639, the oldest continuous series); Anglican/Church of England at Trinity Church (register begins ca. 1698); Presbyterian (First Presbyterian Church, records from ca. 1716); Lutheran; Quaker (Friends) monthly meeting minutes; French Huguenot (Eglise du Saint-Esprit); Shearith Israel (Jewish, burial and congregation records).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, and confirmations. Quaker records include births, deaths, marriages, and disownments. Jewish records include circumcisions and burials.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Church Records, 1640-1940" (Collection ID 1469062) — ~2.3 million records with ~1.1 million images. Date range 1640-1940 covers the colonial period. This is indexed at the state level and searchable by name on FamilySearch at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1469062
- **Volume search result:** One digitized volume was found specifically for New York City in the 1700-1800 window: Image Group 007733180, described as "Dutch Reformed Church Registers," covering 1700-1776, 211 images. This volume is **0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable** — it must be browsed image-by-image. It is in **Dutch**, meaning the researcher must be able to read 18th-century Dutch handwriting and the Dutch language.
- **Language warning:** Dutch Reformed registers throughout the 1700s are in Dutch, even well after the English takeover. Latin was used in some Anglican registers for formal entries. Researchers who cannot read these languages should seek published transcriptions or hire a specialist.
- **Where held:** Original registers are held variously by the New York Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYGBS), the New-York Historical Society, individual parish archives, the Reformed Church in America Archives (New Brunswick Theological Seminary, NJ), and the FamilySearch Catalog microfilm collection.

### Census records

- **Federal/national census:** The first federal census was taken in 1790, at the very end of the colonial/Revolutionary era. It is available and indexed. There are no federal censuses for the 1700s before 1790.
- **Colonial-era enumerations:** Several provincial censuses and tax-based enumerations were taken during the British colonial period. The 1703, 1712, 1723, 1731, 1737, 1746, 1749, 1756, and 1771 colonial censuses of New York Province are known — these are head-of-household lists or fuller enumerations depending on the year. Their survival and digitization status varies; the wiki_search result from the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records) confirms that tax assessment lists survive for some years and wards.
- **Tax lists as census substitutes:** Ward-level tax assessment lists survive for portions of the 1700s and function as inter-censal population listings. The FamilySearch collection "New York, Tax Assessment Rolls of Real and Personal Estates, 1799-1804" (Collection ID 1678432, ~123,000 records, ~61,000 images) covers the tail end of the period.
- **Access:** The 1790 federal census is indexed and searchable online (FamilySearch, Ancestry). Earlier colonial enumerations are largely browse-only or physical-only; consult the New York State Archives (Albany) and the New-York Historical Society for surviving originals.

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills, letters of administration, estate inventories, guardianship appointments, and distribution accounts.
- **Jurisdictional level:** During the colonial period, probate in New York Province was administered by the **Prerogative Court of New York** (a provincial, not county, court). This is a critical distinction: colonial-era wills were proved at the provincial level, not the county courthouse. The New-York Historical Society published a multi-volume series, *Abstracts of Wills on File in the Surrogate's Office, City of New York*, which indexes colonial probate. The wiki_search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records confirms this series exists.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Probate Records, 1629-1971" (Collection ID 1542780) — ~987,000 records with ~493,000 images, spanning from 1629 through the colonial period and beyond. Searchable on FamilySearch at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542780
- **Where held:** New York County Surrogate's Court (original wills post-Revolution); New York State Archives (Albany) holds earlier colonial series; the New-York Historical Society holds the published abstracts.
- **Note on testate vs. intestate:** Wills (testate) are indexed in the Abstracts series. If your ancestor died intestate (without a will), search the administration records in the same Prerogative Court series — a grant of administration names the widow/heirs.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** New York used a **metes and bounds** system, not the later federal rectangular survey. Colonial grants were issued as royal patents or manorial grants.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** During the colonial period, land grants (patents) were issued by the royal governor of New York Province on behalf of the Crown. The New York State Archives holds the original patent series. The FamilySearch collection "New York, Land Records, 1630-1975" (Collection ID 2078654) — ~1.5 million records with ~783,000 images — covers from 1630 onward and is searchable at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078654
- **Types:** Royal patents, manorial grants, deeds of conveyance, mortgages, and city lot surveys. City-level conveyances in Manhattan were recorded by the city clerk.
- **Where held:** New York State Archives (Albany) for colonial patents; New York County Clerk's Office (Manhattan) for deed books; FamilySearch digitized collection for indexed records.
- **Tax records:** Ward-level assessment rolls (personal property and real estate) survive for some years; the New York City Municipal Archives holds many of these.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Queen Anne's War (1702-1713), King George's War (1744-1748), French and Indian War (1754-1763), American Revolutionary War (1775-1783 — though New York City was under British occupation 1776-1783, so both Loyalist and Patriot service records are relevant).
- **Record types:** Provincial militia rolls (New York Province maintained militia lists naming men of military age — the FamilySearch Wiki result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records confirms these survive); Revolutionary War service records and pension files at NARA; Loyalist claims filed with the British government after the war (held at The National Archives, Kew, and Library and Archives Canada).
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington DC and New York regional) for Revolutionary-era federal records; New York State Archives (Albany) for provincial militia; The National Archives (UK) for Loyalist and Crown records.
- **Access:** Revolutionary War pension files are digitized on Fold3 (subscription) and NARA's Access to Archival Databases (free). Provincial militia rolls are largely physical or microfilm only.

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** Trinity Church burial ground (Manhattan, one of the oldest surviving burial grounds in the US, 1680s onward); St. Paul's Chapel burial ground (Anglican, 1766); Dutch Reformed churchyards; Shearith Israel cemetery (the oldest Jewish cemetery in the US, 1656); Friends (Quaker) burial grounds.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has coverage for Trinity Church and other major Manhattan colonial burial grounds — many stones have been photographed and transcribed.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers are held by the individual churches and by the New-York Historical Society. Trinity Church has published its burial records in indexed volumes.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** The *New-York Gazette* (founded 1725, the city's first newspaper) and later the *New-York Weekly Journal* (1733), *New-York Mercury* (1752), and *New-York Journal* (1766) all published marriage and death notices for notable families, plus legal notices (land sales, estate advertisements, runaway servant/enslaved person notices).
- **Where held:** The New-York Historical Society and New York Public Library hold microfilm runs. Some issues are digitized on Chronicling America (Library of Congress, free) and Newspapers.com (subscription, https://www.newspapers.com/).
- **Content value:** Marriage and death notices in colonial newspapers typically covered only elite or prominent families. Legal notices — estate administrator notices, land sale announcements — are more broadly useful. Runaway-servant and enslaved-person notices sometimes provide the only surviving physical descriptions and family relationships of enslaved individuals.

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Relevant ports:** New York Harbor was the primary port of entry for the city. Immigrants arriving via Albany (up the Hudson) also passed through.
- **Record types for the colonial period:** Systematic federal passenger lists did not begin until 1820. For the 1700s, researchers should consult: ship manifests and port records held at the New York State Archives; published transcriptions of colonial immigration lists (e.g., published lists of Dutch and German immigrants); naturalization records filed in the Mayor's Court or the colonial Supreme Court of New York.
- **Naturalization:** Colonial-era naturalizations could be granted by the provincial legislature as well as by courts. Published abstracts exist for some series. The FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records) confirms that Mayor's Court records survive as a key source.
- **Access:** Largely physical or microfilm. Some have been transcribed and published by the New York Genealogical & Biographical Society.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Ward-level personal property and real estate assessment rolls.
- **Date range:** Portions survive for the colonial period; the FamilySearch collection "New York, Tax Assessment Rolls of Real and Personal Estates, 1799-1804" (Collection ID 1678432) begins at the very end of the 1700s.
- **Where held:** New York City Municipal Archives holds the bulk of city-level assessment rolls; New York State Archives (Albany) holds provincial-level tax records.
- **Substitute value:** Ward tax lists from the 1740s-1780s can identify residents between colonial censuses and link them to a specific ward of the city.

### Other record types

- **Court records:** The Mayor's Court of New York City heard civil cases, minor criminal matters, and naturalizations. Minutes and case files survive at the New York City Municipal Archives and the New York State Archives. These name ordinary residents in debt suits, contract disputes, and petitions. The FamilySearch Wiki result (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records) identifies Mayor's Court records as a key colonial source.
- **Colonial Manuscripts:** The New York Colonial Manuscripts at the New York State Archives are a large collection of administrative, land, and legal documents from the Dutch and British periods. Published calendars and indexes exist.
- **Enslaved persons:** Records of enslaved individuals in colonial New York are scattered across multiple series: slaveholder estates in probate records (where enslaved persons are listed as property), manumission records (freedom papers, especially post-1785), church registers (some enslaved persons were baptized and listed by first name), newspaper notices, and the 1790 federal census (which counts enslaved persons by number, not name, in slaveholder households). The New-York Historical Society has collected relevant materials.
- **Town and county histories:** Published 19th-century local histories of New York County often transcribed colonial records and listed founding families. The New York Genealogical & Biographical Record (NYGBR, the journal of NYGBS) published many original-record transcriptions covering the 1700s.

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | New York, Church Records, 1640-1940 (ID 1469062; ~2.3M records); New York, Land Records, 1630-1975 (ID 2078654; ~1.5M records); New York, Probate Records, 1629-1971 (ID 1542780; ~987K records); New York, Tax Assessment Rolls, 1799-1804 (ID 1678432; ~123K records) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census collection including 1790; additional New York state collections | Subscription |

| Chronicling America (loc.gov) | Some digitized colonial New York newspaper runs | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** The `volume_search` query returned 1 digitized volume total (the Dutch Reformed Church Registers, Image Group 007733180, 211 images, 1700-1776, browse-only). This is the complete result set for the specific city-level query. The broader `collections_search` at the state level returned 5 collections — these are the indexed, named-searchable collections on FamilySearch. Additional volumes covering New York City at the state or broader level may exist; researchers should search the FamilySearch Catalog directly by place.

### Physical repositories

| New York City Municipal Archives (31 Chambers St, Manhattan) | City-level administrative records, tax rolls, Mayor's Court records, vital records from the late 1800s onward | In-person; some records on microfilm; online catalog |
| New York State Archives (Albany) | Colonial Manuscripts, land patent series, provincial court records, militia records | In-person; online finding aids; some digitized |
| New-York Historical Society (170 Central Park West) | Church record transcriptions, colonial newspaper runs, Abstracts of Wills series, Loyalist materials | In-person with membership; reading room by appointment |
| New York Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYGBS) | Largest genealogical library in the Northeast; colonial NYC records, NYGB Record journal transcriptions | In-person; some materials digitized for members |
| New York Public Library (NYPL) — Milstein Division | Microfilm of church registers, newspapers, published local histories, city directories | In-person; some digitized |
| Trinity Church Archives (Broadway at Wall St) | Original Anglican/Episcopal registers from ca. 1698; burial records | By appointment |
| Reformed Church in America Archives (New Brunswick, NJ) | Dutch Reformed registers from New York congregations | By appointment |
| The National Archives, Kew (London, UK) | Loyalist claims, British military records for the occupation period, colonial administrative correspondence | In-person or document copies by mail; some records on Fold3 |

---

## Records NOT online

The following record types are known to exist for colonial New York City but are not fully available in any online database:

- **Provincial/colonial census enumerations (1703-1771):** Surviving originals are largely physical at the New York State Archives; few have been digitized or indexed.
- **Mayor's Court minute books and case files:** Not digitized; physical at the New York City Municipal Archives and New York State Archives.
- **Ward tax assessment rolls before 1799:** Physical at the New York City Municipal Archives; not in any online searchable database.
- **Colonial Manuscripts series (New York State Archives):** Published calendars exist, but the originals themselves are physical; only portions have been digitized.
- **Dutch Reformed Church registers for congregations outside the one digitized FamilySearch volume:** Additional registers may be held at the Reformed Church in America Archives and are not yet fully online.
- **Loyalist claims and British military records:** Held at The National Archives (Kew); some are on Fold3 but coverage for the New York City period is incomplete.
- **Manumission and freedom records for enslaved persons:** Scattered across multiple repositories; no consolidated online database.

---

## Known record losses

- **Revolutionary War disruption (1776-1783):** British occupation of New York City for the entire war caused significant disruption to civil record-keeping. Patriot-held records were evacuated or destroyed; some church registers have gaps corresponding to the occupation years.
- **Great Fire of New York (1776):** A major fire in September 1776, shortly after the British landed, destroyed a significant portion of lower Manhattan, including some records held in private and public buildings.
- **General fragmentation of the colonial period:** Colonial-era record-keeping was inconsistent and record survival is uneven. Many records were kept in personal possession of church ministers or local officials and were lost when they died or moved. There is no complete substitute series for missing colonial baptismal or burial records.
- **Enslaved persons:** Because enslaved individuals were generally not recorded as legal persons in colonial records, their genealogical documentation is severely limited. Church baptisms, probate inventories, newspaper notices, and DNA testing are the primary avenues.

---

## Research tips

- **Church registers are the foundation for the 1700s.** Since civil registration did not exist, every vital event research question must begin with church records. Identify the denomination of the family before anything else — Dutch Reformed, Anglican, Presbyterian, and Jewish families used different registers held in different repositories. ([FamilySearch Wiki — New York City Genealogy: Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))
- **The Dutch Reformed register on FamilySearch must be browsed in Dutch.** Image Group 007733180 (Dutch Reformed Church Registers, 1700-1776, 211 images) is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable. You must browse it image by image. The entries are in Dutch. Published transcriptions of the Dutch Reformed registers exist and should be consulted before attempting to browse the images.
- **Wills were proved at the provincial level, not the county courthouse.** Search the *Abstracts of Wills* series published by the New-York Historical Society (indexed by name) before visiting the Surrogate's Court. The FamilySearch collection "New York, Probate Records, 1629-1971" (Collection ID 1542780) is also searchable online. ([FamilySearch Wiki — New York City Genealogy: Tax and Military Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records))
- **The four-wiki-place-page sections for New York State all returned only a generic fallback page, not a New York-specific page.** This is a known data gap for this tool and period. Consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_Genealogy for research strategy.
- **Distinguish colonial New York City (Manhattan/New York County) from the surrounding counties.** Brooklyn was Kings County, across the ferry. A family near the river generated records in Kings County, not New York County. Search both. Similarly, upper Manhattan events may have involved Westchester County.
- **Dutch families used patronymic naming through much of the 1600s and into the early 1700s.** A man named Pieter Jansen had a father named Jan, and his children would use "Pieterse" or "Petersz" as their surname. Patronymics were gradually replaced by fixed surnames during the early 1700s. Searching for a fixed surname will miss earlier generations recorded under the patronymic form. ([FamilySearch Wiki — New York City Genealogy: Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))
- **Huguenot families are well documented.** The Huguenot Society of America and the NYGBS have published transcriptions and compiled genealogies of New York's French Protestant families, many of whom settled in the late 1600s and are traceable through the 1700s.
- **Provincial militia rolls are an underused source.** These list men of military age and can place a person in a specific ward or precinct in a given year, even when no church record survives. ([FamilySearch Wiki — New York City Genealogy: Tax and Military Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records))
- **Research sequence for colonial New York City:** (1) Establish denomination and search the appropriate church register; (2) search probate (Prerogative Court series) for wills and administrations; (3) search land records and the Colonial Manuscripts for property transactions; (4) check ward tax lists for presence in the city; (5) search published local histories and the NYGB Record for transcribed materials; (6) if near the Revolutionary period, determine Loyalist or Patriot alignment and search the appropriate military and claims records.
- **The New York Genealogical & Biographical Record** (the NYGBS journal) is one of the most important finding tools for colonial New York City families. It has published original transcriptions of church registers, court records, and family genealogies for over 150 years. Many pre-1923 issues are freely available online through HathiTrust.

---

*Project note: This locality survey was not persisted to the active research.json because the project's subject (Patrick Flynn, ca. 1845 Pennsylvania) is unrelated to colonial New York City. No `loc_` entry was written so as not to pollute that project's localities with an unrelated survey.*

---

Researching 1700s New York City means working almost entirely without civil vital records — no birth, marriage, or death registration existed for that era. The key records are church registers (especially Dutch Reformed, Anglican at Trinity, and Presbyterian), provincial probate wills proved before the Prerogative Court, colonial land patents, ward-level tax lists, Mayor's Court files, and provincial militia rolls. Most of these survive in physical repositories: the New York City Municipal Archives, the New York State Archives in Albany, the New-York Historical Society, and the New York Genealogical & Biographical Society. Only a handful of record sets are fully name-indexed online, and the one digitized Dutch Reformed church register volume on FamilySearch must be browsed image-by-image and is written entirely in Dutch.

The recommended next step is to identify which religious denomination your family belonged to, then locate that congregation's surviving registers — that single decision determines which repository to approach first and what language the records will be in.

output.text_response:
## Virginia Revolutionary War Records Guide (1775–1783)

Here is a comprehensive locality guide for tracing Virginia families connected to Revolutionary War military service and wartime activities:

---

### Jurisdiction Overview

Virginia was one of the original Thirteen Colonies, operating as a Commonwealth from 1776 onward, with county-level record-keeping dating to the 1630s — making it one of the most thoroughly documented colonial jurisdictions in North America. Richmond became the state capital in 1780 (Williamsburg served before that). Virginia contributed more troops than any other colony to the Continental Army.

**Note on boundaries:** The county map was actively changing during the war. Always verify a county's formation date before searching its records. Kentucky County was created from Virginia in 1776 (Kentucky became its own state in 1792), so far-western families may have records under predecessor Virginia counties.

---

### Key Record Types

#### 🪖 Military Records — Highest Priority for Your Research

**Continental Army / Virginia Continental Line:**
- **Service records & muster rolls:** National Archives (NARA), Record Group 93
- **Pension & bounty-land warrant applications:** NARA, Record Group 15 — **the richest genealogical source of the period**, often containing a veteran's birthplace, parents, wife's name, marriage date/place, children's names/ages, and neighbor depositions
- **Online access:** Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com) for pension files and service records; also partially on Ancestry

**Virginia Militia:**
- Held at the **Library of Virginia** in Richmond (less complete than Continental records)
- FamilySearch collection: "Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783" — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1945678

**Virginia State Navy:**
- Virginia maintained its own state navy; published transcriptions available in print but not comprehensively digitized

**Post-War Bounty Lands (Virginia Military District, Ohio):**
- Virginia granted bounty lands in Ohio to veterans; warrant and survey records connecting veterans to land claims are at the Library of Virginia
- FamilySearch digitized volume of bounty warrants (1779–1800): image group 005301447 (341 images) — browse-only, not name-indexed

---

#### 📜 Tax Lists — Critical Census Substitute

Virginia's 1790 federal census is **largely destroyed** (British burned Washington in 1814). The **1782–1785 personal property tax lists** are the accepted genealogical substitute:
- FamilySearch: "Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850" (collection ID 1456723)
- FamilySearch volume: image group 005301449 (87 images, 1782–1799) — full-text searchable but not name-indexed

---

#### ⛪ Church Records — Only Vital Records Available for This Period

There was **no civil registration** of births, marriages, or deaths in 1775–1783. Church records are the primary source:
- Anglican/Episcopal vestry books (baptisms, marriages, burials — through 1786 disestablishment)
- Baptist, Presbyterian, Methodist, Lutheran, German Reformed registers (especially in the Shenandoah Valley)
- FamilySearch: "Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929" — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598230
- Also at the Library of Virginia and Episcopal Diocese of Virginia archives (Richmond)

---

#### 🏛️ County Court Records

- Wills, administrations, inventories, deed books, marriage bonds, and **court order books** (recording militia musters, supply impressments, local appointments)
- FamilySearch: "Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920" and "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900"
- Augusta County court order books (1775–1795): image group 005301448 (158 images, **61% name-indexed**) — valuable for Shenandoah Valley families
- **Warning:** Many county courthouses suffered 19th-century fires — check the Library of Virginia's "burned counties" documentation before concluding a record never existed

---

#### 🗺️ Land Records

- Virginia is a **state-land state** — do NOT search the BLM/GLO; go to the Library of Virginia instead
- Land patents, deed books, and bounty land warrants
- FamilySearch: "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900"
- Metes-and-bounds deeds name neighboring landowners — useful for identifying relatives and associates

---

#### Other Wartime Sources

- **Loyalist confiscation records:** Forfeiture proceedings against loyalists at the Library of Virginia name family members
- **Virginia Gazette (Williamsburg):** The main wartime newspaper — military notices, estate notices, loyalist lists, death notices; digitized at Accessible Archives
- **DAR Patriot Index:** Finding aid at dar.org confirming documented service and pointing to source records

---

### Repository Summary

| Repository | Key Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Military, church, land, tax, court records | Free |
| **Fold3** | Pension files (RG 15); service records (RG 93) | Subscription |
| **Ancestry** | Pension/bounty-land applications; county records | Subscription |
| **Library of Virginia (Richmond)** | Militia records; state land office; bounty warrants; Virginia Gazette | In-person / lva.virginia.gov |
| **NARA (Washington DC)** | Continental Army service records; pension files | In-person / Fold3 / Ancestry |
| **FindAGrave** | Cemetery transcriptions statewide | Free |
| **Virginia county courthouses** | Original deed, will, order books | In-person or written request |
| **Episcopal Diocese of Virginia archives** | Anglican vestry books and parish registers | Contact directly |

---

### Research Strategy

1. **Start with pension files** on Fold3 — the single richest source, often containing full family data
2. **Use 1782–1785 tax lists** as the census substitute (destroyed 1790 census)
3. **Search church records** for any vital event (baptism, marriage, burial)
4. **Identify the specific county** your ancestor lived in, then target that county's deed books, will books, and court order books
5. **Check bounty land records** if the ancestor later moved to Ohio — the Virginia Military District connection links veterans across state lines
6. **Don't overlook court order books** — militia musters and supply impressments name ordinary people who appear nowhere else

# Locality Guide: Virginia, United States (1775–1783)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** Virginia was one of the original Thirteen Colonies; it achieved statehood in 1788, though it operated as a commonwealth government from 1776 onward during the Revolution. County-level record-keeping dates to the 1630s, making it one of the most thoroughly documented colonial jurisdictions in North America.
- **Administrative center:** Richmond (state capital from 1780; Williamsburg served before that)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** British Crown / Colony of Virginia until 1776; Commonwealth of Virginia thereafter
- **Population during period:** No population data was returned by the population tool for this specific time window. According to Wikipedia, Virginia contributed more troops than any other colony to the Continental Army, suggesting a substantial population base.
- **Economy:** Tobacco agriculture, some grain farming, iron forging, and maritime trade along the Chesapeake Bay and its tributaries
- **Ethnic composition:** English-descended majority; also Scots-Irish (especially in the Shenandoah Valley and western counties), German settlers (Shenandoah), African-descended enslaved people (large proportion throughout tidewater and piedmont), and smaller Welsh and French Huguenot communities
- **Religious denominations:** Anglican/Church of England (the established church through 1786), Presbyterian (especially in the Valley), Baptist (growing rapidly during this period), Methodist, Lutheran, and German Reformed (western counties)
- **Key historical events:** The war itself was fought partly on Virginia soil — the Yorktown campaign (1781) ended British resistance. Virginia supplied the Continental Army with soldiers, supplies, and leadership. The Anglican establishment was disestablished by the Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom (1786), affecting church record continuity.

## Boundary changes

Virginia's boundaries were broadly stable during 1775–1783, but the county map was actively changing. New counties were carved from existing ones throughout the war years; whenever you identify a county for an ancestor, verify the county's formation date to confirm it existed at the time of the event. Records belong to the county that existed at the date of the event, not the county a place falls in today. Kentucky County was created from Virginia in 1776, and Kentucky became a separate state in 1792; families in far southwestern or western Virginia may have records under predecessor Virginia counties.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** Virginia did NOT have statewide civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths during the Revolutionary War period. The FamilySearch Wiki page for Virginia Vital Records was not returned by the wiki tool in a Virginia-specific form, so a precise statewide registration start year cannot be cited here. Based on the FamilySearch Wiki's general guidance on US states, statewide registration typically came in the late 1800s or early 1900s — consult the Virginia Vital Records page at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Vital_Records directly for the exact date and level.
- **What exists:** For 1775–1783, births, marriages, and deaths were NOT systematically registered by civil authority. The primary sources are:
  - County court marriage bonds and registers (held at the county courthouse and partly digitized)
  - Anglican/Episcopal vestry books (recording baptisms and burials through 1786 when the establishment ended)
  - Dissenting church registers (Baptist, Presbyterian, Methodist)
- **Where held:** Library of Virginia (Richmond) and individual county courthouses; many have been microfilmed by FamilySearch
- **Gaps:** The end of the Anglican establishment in 1786 created a gap in parish record-keeping; dissenting church records vary enormously in survival

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Anglican/Episcopal (vestry books), Baptist, Presbyterian, Methodist, Lutheran, German Reformed
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages (including marriage bonds filed with county courts), burials, confirmations, and some poor-relief lists in vestry books
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929" (collection ID 1598230) covers this period. The collection spans 1680–1929 and overlaps the war years fully.
- **Digitization level:** This collection is indexed and has images online at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598230
- **Where else held:** Library of Virginia; Episcopal Diocese of Virginia archives (Richmond); local churches
- **Language:** English throughout

### Census records

- **Federal census:** The first federal census was 1790 — outside the war period, but very useful immediately afterward to locate families. **Critical gap:** Virginia's 1790 federal census was largely destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814. The 1782–1785 state enumerations (personal property tax lists) are the standard substitute.
- **State enumerations / tax lists (1782–1785):** These function as a near-census for the immediate post-war years. FamilySearch has a digitized volume (image group 005301449, 87 images, covering 1782–1799) that is **full-text searchable but 0% name-indexed** — it can be searched by text but not browsed by name through a standard name search.
- **Access:** Browse-only / full-text searchable; see also the FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850" (collection ID 1456723).

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, and estate distributions filed at the county court level. County court order books also recorded militia musters, road assignments, and local business — useful for placing an ancestor in a county even without a direct vital or land record.
- **FamilySearch collections:** "Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920" (collection ID 2134567) and "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900" (collection ID 1734285) both cover the war period.
- **Digitized volume:** Augusta County court order books (1775–1795), image group 005301448, 158 images, **61% name-indexed** — partially searchable by name.
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images for the Augusta volume; the broader collections are indexed + images online at the FamilySearch URLs above.
- **Where held:** County courthouses (originals); Library of Virginia (many have been transferred or microfilmed)

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Virginia is a state-land state; land grants issued by the colonial and then state government, not the federal government)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The Virginia Land Office (colonial; then Commonwealth of Virginia Land Office after 1776). The Virginia State Library / Library of Virginia holds these grants and patents.
- **Types:** Land patents and grants, deed books (recorded at the county courthouse), bounty land warrants for Revolutionary War service
- **Bounty land warrants:** Virginia granted bounty lands in the Virginia Military District of Ohio to veterans. Warrant and survey records connecting veterans to their land claims are at the Virginia State Library. FamilySearch has a digitized volume of Revolutionary War land bounty warrants (1779–1800), image group 005301447, 341 images, **0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — browse-only**.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900" (collection ID 1734285) includes deed and will records from this period.
- **Digitization level:** Bounty warrant volume is browse-only (must be examined image by image); the broader land/marriage/will collection is indexed + images online.

### Military records

This is the core record group for your research.

**Continental Army / Virginia Continental Line:**
- Service records and muster rolls are at the National Archives (NARA), Record Group 93. These document soldiers in the Continental Army proper.
- Pension and bounty-land warrant applications are at NARA, Record Group 15. These are among the richest genealogical records of the period — pension applications often include detailed biographical statements, family data, and witness depositions.
- **Online access:** Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com) holds digitized Revolutionary War pension files and service records. NARA's online catalog also links to some digitized series.

**Virginia Militia:**
- Virginia militia records are held at the Library of Virginia in Richmond. These document men who served in county militia units rather than the Continental Line. Coverage is less complete than the Continental records.

**FamilySearch collection:** "Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783" (collection ID 1945678) covers the war years exactly, with records spanning that date range.
- Access: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1945678

**Virginia State Navy:**
- Virginia maintained its own state navy during the war. Published Virginia State Navy records document naval service.

**Pension files — highest genealogical value:** Pension applications submitted after the war (especially under the Acts of 1818 and 1832) frequently contain a veteran's birthplace, parents, siblings, wife's name, marriage date and place, children's names and ages, and statements from neighbors. These are searchable on Fold3 and are partially available through Ancestry as well.

**Post-war bounty lands (Virginia Military District, Ohio):** The wiki_search result specifically identified warrant and survey records at the Virginia State Library as linking veterans to their land claims. These records can trace men who later moved from Virginia to Ohio.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Personal property tax lists (beginning 1782) and land tax lists. These are the primary substitute for the destroyed 1790 Virginia census.
- **Date range:** 1782 onward (the 1782 enumerations are the earliest surviving statewide series)
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850" (collection ID 1456723)
- **FamilySearch volume:** Image group 005301449 (87 images, 1782–1799, full-text searchable but 0% name-indexed)
- **Digitization level:** Full-text searchable but not name-indexed for the volume; the collection record indicates indexing at the collection level — consult both.
- **Substitute value:** Because the 1790 federal Virginia census is largely destroyed, the 1782–1785 tax lists are the genealogical standard substitute for locating families in that decade.

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** Anglican/Episcopal churchyards (often associated with the same parishes whose vestry books recorded baptisms and burials), Baptist and Presbyterian congregation graveyards, and family burial plots on private land — common in rural Virginia
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com) has extensive Virginia listings including colonial-era stones. BillionGraves also has Virginia coverage.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for this period are rare; the church vestry books are the primary burial documentation. Many headstone inscriptions have been transcribed by the DAR and local historical societies.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** The Virginia Gazette (Williamsburg) was published during the war years and is the main newspaper source for the period. It carried military notices, government proclamations, death notices, and lists of deserters and loyalists.
- **Where held:** Colonial Williamsburg Foundation; Library of Virginia; digitized at Accessible Archives and on some state library platforms
- **Content value:** Notices of estates for probate, runaway servants and enslaved people, military appointments, and social news naming individuals not found in official records

### Probate and estate records

- **Types:** Wills, letters of administration, inventories, estate accounts, and guardian bonds
- **Where held:** County courthouse (original books); Library of Virginia holds many transferred series; FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900" (collection ID 1734285) indexes many
- **War-era relevance:** Men who died during the war generated estate records at the county court; surviving widows appear in subsequent guardian and dower proceedings. These can document family structure when vital records are absent.

### Other record types of wartime relevance

- **Loyalist records:** Virginians who remained loyal to the Crown were subject to forfeiture proceedings. Confiscated estate records at the Library of Virginia name both the loyalist and sometimes their family members.
- **County court minute books:** Recorded militia musters, impressment of supplies, appointments of local officers, and road/bridge assignments. These name ordinary people who appear in no other series.
- **DAR patriot indexes:** The Daughters of the American Revolution maintains a patriot index linking known Revolutionary War ancestors to their records. Search at dar.org.
- **Published muster rolls and rosters:** Several published volumes transcribe Virginia Revolutionary War muster rolls. The Library of Virginia and the Virginia Genealogical Society have published guides to these.

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783 (ID 1945678); Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929 (ID 1598230); Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900 (ID 1734285); Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850 (ID 1456723); Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920 (ID 2134567) | Free |
| Fold3 | Revolutionary War pension files (NARA RG 15); Continental Army service records (NARA RG 93) | Subscription |
| Ancestry | US Revolutionary War pension and bounty-land warrant applications; some Virginia county records | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | NARA catalog links to digitized RG 93 and RG 15 series; some free online | Free for catalog; some digitized files free |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery headstone transcriptions and photographs statewide | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers including Virginia Gazette | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 3 digitized volumes total for this place and period across the record types queried, and the nextPageToken was not present — this appears to be the complete set of volumes returned by that query. Additional volumes may exist under different query parameters (e.g., broader record type groups). The collections_search returned 5 indexed collections.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Library of Virginia (Richmond) | Virginia militia records; state land office records; bounty warrant files; county records transferred from courthouses; Virginia Gazette on microfilm | In-person; some online request; lva.virginia.gov |
| National Archives (NARA, Washington DC / College Park) | Continental Army service records (RG 93); pension and bounty-land files (RG 15) | In-person; online via Fold3/Ancestry; written request for copies |
| Virginia county courthouses | Original deed books, will books, court order books, marriage bonds | In-person or written request to the county circuit court clerk |
| Virginia Historical Society (Richmond) | Manuscript collections, family papers, published local histories | In-person; some digitized finding aids online |
| Episcopal Diocese of Virginia archives (Richmond) | Vestry books and parish registers for Anglican/Episcopal parishes | Contact the diocesan archives |
| Virginia Genealogical Society | Published transcriptions, county record guides | Membership; vgs.org |

---

## Records NOT online

The following exist but are not fully available in any online database as of the survey date:

- **Virginia militia records** at the Library of Virginia — these are physically held there and only partially microfilmed or digitized
- **Anglican vestry books** — some are digitized in the church records collection, but many remain on microfilm or in parish/diocesan custody
- **County court minute books** for many counties — the Augusta County volume is partially indexed, but most other counties' wartime-era minutes are not yet fully digitized or indexed
- **Virginia State Navy records** — published transcriptions exist in print but are not fully searchable online
- **Loyalist confiscation/forfeiture records** — held at the Library of Virginia; not comprehensively digitized
- **Original Revolutionary War land bounty warrant files** (image group 005301447, 341 images) — these are digitized but 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable; they must be browsed image by image

---

## Known record losses

- **1790 federal census for Virginia:** Largely destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814. The 1782–1785 personal property tax lists are the standard genealogical substitute. Search "Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850" (FamilySearch collection 1456723) first.
- **County courthouse fires:** Virginia suffered numerous courthouse fires in the 19th century, destroying records for some counties. Among the most seriously affected: Hanover County (1865 fire destroyed many records); check the Library of Virginia's "burned counties" documentation before concluding a record does not exist.
- **Anglican vestry books:** The disestablishment of the Church of England in 1786 disrupted record-keeping. Some vestry books were lost in the transition; others survive in parish, diocesan, or state custody.

---

## Research tips

- **Start with pension files.** For any man suspected of Continental Army or militia service, the pension application file at NARA (searchable on Fold3 at https://www.fold3.com) is the single richest genealogical source. It often contains a biographical statement, wife's name and marriage details, and children's names. The wiki_search result from the FamilySearch Military Records article confirmed pension files are in NARA Record Group 15.
- **Use the 1782–1785 tax lists as a census substitute.** Because Virginia's 1790 census is largely destroyed, the personal property tax lists beginning 1782 are the accepted substitute for locating families in that decade. The FamilySearch wiki_search result confirmed this explicitly (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands).
- **Virginia was a state-land state.** Land grants and patents came from the Commonwealth (or Colony before 1776), not from the federal government. Do not search the Bureau of Land Management / General Land Office for Virginia land grants — go to the Library of Virginia and the Virginia Land Office records instead.
- **Bounty lands in Ohio link Virginia veterans.** The Virginia Military District of Ohio was set aside for Virginia veterans. If an ancestor moved from Virginia to Ohio after the war, search the warrant and survey records at the Library of Virginia as well as Ohio land records. The FamilySearch wiki_search result confirmed these records connect veterans to their land claims (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands).
- **Augusta County records are partially indexed.** The county court order books for Augusta County (1775–1795) are 61% name-indexed in FamilySearch (image group 005301448). Augusta County covered a large swath of the Shenandoah Valley during the war — if your ancestors were in the Valley, this volume is directly searchable by name.
- **Check adjoining jurisdictions.** Virginia's western counties (what is now West Virginia and Kentucky) were carved from Virginia during and after the war. Families in border areas may have records under predecessor counties. Kentucky County (created 1776 from Fincastle County) and later Kentucky District counties hold records for families who were technically Virginians during the war but whose records are filed under those geographic units.
- **Church records fill the vital records gap.** There was no civil vital registration during 1775–1783. Anglican vestry books (baptisms, marriages, burials) and dissenting church registers are the only systematic vital records for this period. Begin with the FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929" (ID 1598230) for anything touching baptisms, marriages, or burials.
- **The DAR Patriot Index is a compiled finding aid.** It does not replace original records, but it can confirm a man's service was documented and point to the source records.
- **Metes-and-bounds deeds name neighbors.** Because Virginia used metes and bounds (describing land by reference to neighbors' tracts and natural features), deed books frequently name surrounding landowners — a valuable way to identify associates and relatives of your ancestor.

---

---

This guide covers Virginia during 1775–1783, the years of the American Revolutionary War. For this period, Virginia had no civil birth, marriage, or death registration — families appear instead through church records (Anglican vestry books and dissenting registers), county court records (deed books, will books, order books, marriage bonds), and the personal property tax lists that begin in 1782 and substitute for the largely-destroyed 1790 federal census. The most important military sources — Continental Army service records and pension application files at the National Archives — are searchable through Fold3 and Ancestry and are frequently the richest biographical records available, often naming a veteran's birthplace, wife, children, and neighbors. The Library of Virginia in Richmond holds Virginia militia records and state land office records that are not fully online. One significant caution: many Virginia county courthouse records were destroyed by 19th-century fires, so if a county record cannot be found, check the Library of Virginia's burned-counties documentation before concluding it never existed.

The logical next step is to identify the specific Virginia county where your ancestor lived, then narrow the record search to that county's courthouse holdings, the relevant church denomination, and that county's portion of the tax lists and deed books.

Here is the locality guide's response on New Orleans early-1800s records, disaster survival, and where to look for copies and substitutes:

---

# Locality Guide: New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana (Early 1800s, c. 1800–1860)

## Known Record Losses — The Central Issue

Multiple disasters caused severe record loss in New Orleans:

**1788 Great Fire:** Destroyed ~856 structures. Most French colonial-era civic records held in the Cabildo and private homes were lost. However, St. Louis Cathedral's sacramental registers — some dating to 1731 — survived because the church maintained its own separate custody.

**1794 Second Fire:** Destroyed additional civic and private records.

**Ongoing environmental damage:** New Orleans's below-sea-level position, subtropical humidity, hurricanes, and periodic floods have degraded paper records across every institution. Yellow fever epidemics (1832, 1853, and others) strained record-keeping systems.

| Disaster | What was lost | Substitute sources |
|---|---|---|
| Great Fire 1788 | Most French colonial civic records | Spanish-era Cabildo records that survived; church registers held separately; notarial copies |
| Second Fire 1794 | Additional civic and private records | Notarial archives; church registers |
| Yellow fever epidemics | Mass mortality; gapped burial registers | Newspaper death notices; published mortality statistics |
| Hurricanes and floods | Periodic damage across all institutions | Microfilm copies made before damage; FamilySearch digitization projects |

**Critical point:** Because notaries were required to keep their own registers *and* the state maintained parallel copies, some notarial transactions survive even when civic records for the same period were destroyed. The notarial archives functioned as a **distributed backup system** that the fire-prone civic record offices did not — making them the single most important repository for early-1800s New Orleans research.

---

## What Survived and Where to Find It

### Church Records (Most Important Starting Point)
- St. Louis Cathedral's sacramental registers survive from **1731** (with gaps)
- **FamilySearch collection 1612905** — "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" — indexed with images; ~987,654 records
- ⚠️ Separate registers were kept for **white parishioners**, **free persons of color**, and **enslaved persons** — searching only one series will produce false negatives
- Originals held at the **Archdiocesan Archives of New Orleans**

### Notarial Records (Unique to Louisiana's Civil Law System)
- The **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** holds **30+ million pages** dating to 1734 — an extraordinary survival given the fires
- Covers manumissions (freedom papers), marriage contracts, property sales, apprenticeships, and more
- FamilySearch has only **one browse-only volume** (imageGroupNumber 004990115, 1803–1820, 167 images, 0% indexed) — the vast majority requires **in-person access** at 1340 Poydras Street, New Orleans

### Probate / Successions (Louisiana term)
- **FamilySearch collection 2078341** — "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984" — indexed with images
- Successions name heirs, establish family relationships, and often list enslaved persons by name — crucial for family reconstruction when vital records are missing

### Civil Vital Records
- Louisiana did not have early systematic civil registration; for the early 1800s, **church registers are the primary source**
- **FamilySearch collection 1543892** — "Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964" — index only, no images
- Civil marriages: **FamilySearch collection 1798054** — "Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837–1957" — begins 1837

### Census Records
- Federal census coverage begins with **1810** (Louisiana admitted as a state 1812); earlier censuses did not cover Louisiana
- 1850 and 1860 slave schedules list enslaved persons by age/sex only (no names) under the enslaver's name — pair with church registers, notarial acts, and succession records for names

### Newspapers (especially for enslaved persons)
- **Runaway slave advertisements** in papers like the *Louisiana Gazette* (1804+) and *New Orleans Bee* (1827+) name enslaved individuals with physical descriptions, stated origins, and language skills
- Available on Newspapers.com and GenealogyBank (subscriptions)

### Passenger Lists
- New Orleans was the second-largest U.S. port of entry in this period
- Federal manifest requirements began **1820**; pre-1820 arrivals require contact with **NARA Southeast Region, Atlanta**

## Repository Guide

| Repository | Key Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (free) | Church records (1612905), probate (2078341), marriages (1798054), death index (1543892) | Online free |
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | 30M+ pages of notarial acts from 1734 | In-person only |
| Archdiocesan Archives of New Orleans | Cathedral sacramental registers from 1731 | In-person or written inquiry |
| Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge | Territorial/state records, land records, successions | In-person; some digitized |
| NARA Southeast Region, Atlanta | Passenger lists, federal court records, military | In-person; some at archives.gov |
| Ancestry (subscription) | Federal censuses, passenger lists | Online subscription |
| Newspapers.com / GenealogyBank | Historical New Orleans newspapers | Online subscription |

---

## Key Research Tips

1. **Start with church registers**, not civil records — for any event before the late 1830s, collection 1612905 is far more likely to document it.
2. **Check all three register series** at St. Louis Cathedral — white, free persons of color, and enslaved — based on the ancestor's legal status at the time.
3. **Go to the Notarial Archives for almost everything else** — manumissions, property, marriage contracts, business transactions. The in-person visit is essential; FamilySearch's digitized portion is a tiny fraction.
4. **Records are in French and Spanish**, not English — most early-1800s church and notarial records require French-language ability or translation assistance.
5. **A negative result is not a finding** — given the fires of 1788 and 1794 and distributed records across multiple institutions, absence in one database never establishes absence of documentation. Work all surviving series.
6. **Check neighboring parishes** (St. Bernard, Jefferson, St. Tammany) for families living near parish boundaries.

---

The bottom line: New Orleans experienced catastrophic record losses in 1788 and 1794, but remarkable survivals remain — St. Louis Cathedral registers going back to 1731, 30+ million pages of notarial acts, and rich probate/succession records. The key to success is knowing *which institutions* held records independently of the destroyed civic offices, and visiting them (especially the Notarial Archives) in person.
