---

# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region (1860-1890)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Counties covered:** Schuylkill (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton), Luzerne (formed 1786), Lackawanna (formed 1878 from Luzerne), Carbon (formed 1843 from Monroe and Northampton), Northumberland (formed 1772)
- **County seats:** Pottsville (Schuylkill), Wilkes-Barre (Luzerne), Scranton (Lackawanna), Jim Thorpe / Mauch Chunk (Carbon), Sunbury (Northumberland)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period (Schuylkill County, confirmed by census data):** 89,510 (1860) → 116,428 (1870) → 129,974 (1880). Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, and Northumberland counties show comparable rapid growth driven by coal extraction.
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining dominated all five counties. Collieries, breaker operations, company-owned patch towns, canal transport (Schuylkill Canal, Lehigh Canal), and railroad haulage (Philadelphia and Reading Railroad; Delaware, Lackawanna and Western) defined daily life and employment.
- **Ethnic composition:** Large Irish immigrant population, especially post-Famine arrivals of 1845-1855 who were working adult miners through the 1860s-1890s. Welsh miners concentrated in Luzerne and Lackawanna. German settlers. Eastern European (Slovak, Polish, Lithuanian) populations growing by the late 1880s.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant among Irish, with parishes founded 1840-1870); Welsh Calvinist Methodist; Presbyterian; Lutheran; German Reformed; Episcopal.
- **Key historical events:** Molly Maguires trials and executions (1877, Schuylkill County); Long Strike of 1875; Pennsylvania Mine Safety Act (1869); formation of Lackawanna County from Luzerne (1878); growth of the Philadelphia and Reading Railroad.

## Boundary changes

- **Lackawanna County formed 1878 from Luzerne County.** This is the single most consequential boundary event for this research window. All records for the Scranton, Carbondale, and surrounding area before 1878 were created and filed under Luzerne County. Search Luzerne County in every record category for events in what is now Lackawanna County before that year.
- **Schuylkill County formed 1811** from Berks and Northampton; no relevant boundary changes within 1860-1890.
- **Carbon County formed 1843** from Monroe and Northampton; stable through the target period.
- **Northumberland County formed 1772;** oldest of the five; stable boundaries.
- **Luzerne County formed 1786;** lost its northern section to form Lackawanna in 1878. Luzerne County records from before 1878 thus cover what is now both Luzerne and Lackawanna counties — they are one continuous research trail despite the different county names.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** Pennsylvania statewide civil registration of births and deaths did **not begin until 1906** at the state level. The entire 1860-1890 target window falls before any statewide registration requirement. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania Vital Records and related sub-topics returned only generic content in this survey, so no Pennsylvania-specific local start dates were confirmed by the tools.
- **What exists in online collections:**
  - Pennsylvania County Marriages, 1885-1950 (FamilySearch collection 1921317; 524,189 indexed records, 312,045 images) — the 1885-1890 slice overlaps the target window.
  - Pennsylvania Civil Marriages, 1677-1950 (collection 1571957; 312,045 indexed records).
  - Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages, 1700-1900 (collection 1502909; 198,765 indexed records, no images).
  - Pennsylvania Death Certificates, 1906-1968 (collection 2255317; 4,218,763 fully indexed records with images) — entirely post-period, but useful for death dates of ancestors who survived into the 1900s.
- **Schuylkill County marriage volume digitized on FamilySearch:** imageGroupNumber 007936753, covering 1870-1910, 94 images — **browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable).
- **Gaps:** No statewide birth or death registration during 1860-1890. Church records are the primary vital-record source for this entire window.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic parish baptismal registers (Diocese of Scranton or Harrisburg); Protestant church registers; newspaper obituaries.

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (most Irish parishes); Welsh Calvinist Methodist; Presbyterian; Lutheran; German Reformed; Episcopal.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations, First Communion records, and status animarum (parish census) books in Catholic parishes.
- **Where held:**
  - Diocese of Scranton (formed 1868): holds records for most Lackawanna and northern Luzerne County parishes from 1868 forward. Contact: Diocese of Scranton Archives, 300 Wyoming Avenue, Scranton, PA 18503.
  - Diocese of Harrisburg: holds records for southern anthracite counties (Schuylkill, Carbon, Northumberland) and for all coal-region parishes before 1868.
  - Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records)), many Catholic parishes in the coal region were established between 1840 and 1870 specifically to serve Irish and Eastern European immigrant communities; baptismal registers from these parishes are the primary Irish-ancestry vital evidence for 1860-1890.
  - FamilySearch digitized Schuylkill County church records: imageGroupNumber 007936751, 1842-1895, 187 images, languages English and German — **browse-only images** (0% indexed, not full-text searchable). Must be examined image by image. German-language entries require reading the original language.
- **Language:** English and German in most entries; Latin in formal Catholic sacramental registers.

### Census records

- **Federal census:** Pennsylvania is covered in all federal decennial censuses. Relevant years for this window: 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900. Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Pennsylvania Genealogy, Census Records section](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania,_United_States_Genealogy#Census_Records)):
  - The **1880 census** is the first to record the relationship of each household member to the head of household — especially valuable for proving family connections.
  - The **1890 population schedules are almost entirely destroyed** nationwide. The 1880 and 1900 censuses bracket this gap.
  - The 1870 and 1900 censuses provide complementary evidence.
- **Mortality schedules:** The federal mortality schedules (1850-1885) record deaths in the year preceding each census — relevant alongside the 1860, 1870, and 1880 enumerations.
- **State/other enumerations:** Pennsylvania triennial tax assessments (see Tax Records below) serve as intercensal substitutes at three-year intervals.
- **External link confirmed by tools:** 1850 United States Federal Census - Schuylkill County on Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/1276/). The 1860-1900 federal censuses are fully indexed on FamilySearch (free) and Ancestry (subscription).

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills (testate estates), letters of administration (intestate estates — the far more common path for a working-class Irish miner who died without a will), guardianship petitions for minor children, inventories, estate distributions.
- **Identifying testate vs. intestate:** For a miner who died without a will, search the administration file, not the will index. Many Irish immigrant miners held no real property and left only personal effects.
- **Date range:** From county formation through the period.
- **Where held and digitization status:**
  - Schuylkill County probate records: FamilySearch imageGroupNumber 007936749, covering 1851-1930, 412 images — **browse-only** (0% indexed, not full-text searchable).
  - Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994 (FamilySearch collection 1999196, 3,200,560 images, 0 indexed records) — images are present but not name-searchable; must be browsed by county/year.
- **Naturalization records (court-held):** Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Pennsylvania Naturalization Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Naturalization_Records)), pre-1906 naturalizations are scattered across county Quarter Sessions, Common Pleas, and Orphans' Courts — not centralized in any single repository. Declarations of intent and petitions for naturalization name the applicant's country of origin — critical for tracing Irish origins.
  - Schuylkill County naturalization records digitized: imageGroupNumber 007936750, 1849-1915, 298 images — **browse-only** (0% indexed, not full-text searchable).
  - After September 1906, naturalization centralized in federal courts; NARA Philadelphia holds eastern Pennsylvania federal naturalizations.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is a state-land state, not a federal-land state).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The Pennsylvania Land Office issued warrants and patents; the county Recorder of Deeds holds deed transfers. Note that colliery company towns meant many Irish miners lived in company-owned housing and did not hold land in their own names — sheriff's sales and mortgage records may be more genealogically relevant than straightforward deeds.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, sheriff's deeds, tax records.
- **Where held and digitization status:**
  - Schuylkill County deed records digitized on FamilySearch: imageGroupNumber 007936752, 1815-1900, 543 images — **22% name-indexed** (partial name search possible, but most images must still be browsed). This is the only partially indexed Schuylkill County volume found in this survey.
- **Tax records:** Pennsylvania state assessors enumerated coal-region residents triennially from 1853, per [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records). Ledgers list householder, real estate value, occupation, and sometimes nativity.
- **External link confirmed by tools:** Pennsylvania, U.S., Tax and Exoneration Lists, 1768-1801 on Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/7667/) — pre-period background only.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861-1865). Irish anthracite miners served heavily in Pennsylvania volunteer infantry regiments.
- **Record types:** Service records and pension files at NARA; Pennsylvania Civil War Muster Rolls at the Pennsylvania State Archives. Pension files are especially valuable: they include age, birthplace, marriage dates, and names of children — often more biographical detail than any other record from this period.
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington, D.C.) for Civil War service and pension records. Pennsylvania State Archives, 350 North Street, Harrisburg, PA 17120. Pension files are digitized on Fold3 and partially on Ancestry.

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** Catholic parish cemeteries attached to Irish-founded parishes in each coal town; non-sectarian borough cemeteries; company-owned cemeteries at some collieries.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave and BillionGraves index many coal-region headstones but coverage is incomplete — physical visits may be needed for smaller parish cemeteries.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records at individual parishes or borough offices; Catholic parish burial registers held at diocesan archives (see Church Records above).

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:**
  - **Miners' Journal** (Pottsville, Schuylkill County, 1825-present) is the single most important paper — it covered the entire anthracite region and published obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices, and trial coverage including the Molly Maguire proceedings. Obituaries in this paper frequently name the deceased's county or townland of origin in Ireland.
  - Scranton Republican and Wilkes-Barre Record (Luzerne/Lackawanna area); Carbon Advocate (Carbon County).
- **Where held:** Miners' Journal historical issues on microfilm at the Schuylkill County Historical Society; partial digitization on Chronicling America (Library of Congress, free at chroniclingamerica.loc.gov).
- **Content value:** Irish immigrant obituaries from the 1870s-1890s often contain place-of-origin information in Ireland that appears in no surviving civil record. This is the highest-value newspaper source for Irish coal-region research.

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia (primary arrival port for Irish immigrants to eastern Pennsylvania); New York (Castle Garden, 1855-1890; Ellis Island from 1892); Baltimore.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists at NARA and Ancestry; naturalization declarations (county courts, pre-1906); passport applications.
- **Where held:** NARA Mid-Atlantic Region (Philadelphia) for Philadelphia port records; NARA New York for New York arrivals. Both are digitized on Ancestry and FamilySearch.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family arrival, examine the full manifest for all family members — children as young as newborns are listed. Post-1895 lists include place of last residence and a contact person at the destination, which can identify the Irish townland or a relative already in Pennsylvania.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Pennsylvania triennial state property assessment ledgers (from 1853); county poor tax; personal property tax.
- **Date range:** Triennial from 1853 onward, covering 1862, 1865, 1868, 1871, 1874, 1877, 1880, 1883, 1886, 1889 within the target window.
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives and individual county courthouses / historical societies. Not widely digitized.
- **Substitute value:** These triennial assessments at regular three-year intervals are the primary intercensal evidence between the 1860, 1870, and 1880 federal censuses, and the primary substitute for the destroyed 1890 census. They verify occupation (specifically identifying "miner" or a colliery role) and sometimes nativity.

### Specialized coal-region indexes

Per [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records) — a FamilySearch Wiki page retrieved directly in this survey:

- **Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855-1898:** Names approximately 41,000 colliery workers across the anthracite field, drawn from company payroll books that survived a 1903 records consolidation. Entries include occupation (loader, breaker boy, mule driver), wage rate, and parish of origin where stated. This is the most direct genealogical finding aid for Irish immigrant miners in the northern anthracite counties (Lackawanna, Luzerne) — especially for individuals whose names were indexed inconsistently in census records.
- **Company payroll indexes vs. mine-inspection reports:** Payroll-derived indexes name individual workers. Mine-inspection and accident reports are organized by colliery, not by person. Use payroll indexes first for a person-level search. Accident reports are still valuable — they name the deceased and witnesses, and a mining death may be the only record that pins a man to a specific colliery on a specific date.

### Other record types

- **Occupational records:** Coal company employment records where they survive; mine inspection reports (Pennsylvania State Archives, organized by colliery); union records (Workingmen's Benevolent Association, 1868-1875; United Mine Workers of America from 1890).
- **Institutional records:** Miners' hospital and dispensary records; county almshouse records (for destitute miners or widows).
- **Town and county histories:** 19th-century published local histories for Schuylkill, Luzerne, and Carbon counties frequently contain biographical sketches of prominent residents and reprint early records no longer held in archives. Available through WorldCat and the FamilySearch Catalog (search by place).

| Fold3 | Civil War service records and pension files | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** 5 digitized volumes match Schuylkill County for the 1860-1890 period; this was the complete result set (totalResults: 5, no further pages). Separate volume searches for Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, and Northumberland counties were not retrieved in this survey — a gap to address by searching those standardPlace values directly on FamilySearch.

| Diocese of Scranton Archives, Scranton, PA | Catholic parish registers for Lackawanna and northern Luzerne parishes (post-1868) | Write or call for access |
| Diocese of Harrisburg Archives, Harrisburg, PA | Catholic parish registers for southern anthracite counties; all coal-region parishes pre-1868 | Write or call for access |

| Luzerne County Historical Society, Wilkes-Barre, PA | Records covering the entire pre-1878 region including what is now Lackawanna County | In-person |

## Records NOT online

- Triennial state tax assessment ledgers for most years (physical at Pennsylvania State Archives and county repositories)
- Pre-1906 naturalization petitions for Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, and Northumberland counties (Schuylkill County volumes are digitized on FamilySearch but browse-only; the other four counties were not retrieved in this survey)
- Most Catholic parish baptismal and burial registers (held at diocesan archives, not publicly digitized)
- Coal company payroll books beyond what is captured in the Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index
- Mine inspection reports and accident records (Pennsylvania State Archives)
- Union records (Workingmen's Benevolent Association; United Mine Workers)
- Miners' Journal full run (only partially digitized on Chronicling America)
- County almshouse and institutional records

## Known record losses

- The **1890 federal census is almost entirely destroyed** nationwide — the most significant gap for tracking a family between 1880 and 1900. Substitutes: triennial tax assessments (1883, 1886, 1889), borough/city directories, church records for life events in those years, and the 1900 census.
- No major courthouse fires for the five coal counties were confirmed by the tool results in this survey. The FamilySearch county-specific genealogy pages returned only generic content, so the question of courthouse fires and local record losses should be verified directly with each county's historical society before assuming all records survive.

## Research tips

- **Start with the Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index** if your ancestor worked in the northern anthracite field (Lackawanna/Luzerne counties): it names approximately 41,000 workers, gives occupation and sometimes parish of origin, and is the most direct path to a specific Irish miner. See [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records).

- **Naturalization records name the country of origin — search every county court.** Before September 1906, a Declaration of Intent or petition for naturalization could be filed in any Pennsylvania court of record. An Irish-born miner may have filed in a county he passed through or worked in briefly, not only where he later settled. Per [Pennsylvania Naturalization Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Naturalization_Records), these documents name the country of origin. For Schuylkill County, FamilySearch imageGroupNumber 007936750 (1849-1915, 298 images) is digitized but must be browsed image by image.

- **Search both dioceses for Catholic records.** An event before 1868 in what is now Lackawanna County falls under the Diocese of Harrisburg, not Scranton. The 1868 diocesan split is a research dividing line that runs parallel to the 1878 county split — both must be tracked.

- **For Lackawanna County events before 1878:** search Luzerne County records in every category — court, probate, church, deed. These are one continuous research trail, not separate record sets. The administrative boundary did not exist; the records were created and filed under Luzerne.

- **Read the Miners' Journal for obituaries.** This Pottsville paper covered the entire anthracite field and frequently named the deceased's townland or county in Ireland — information absent from any civil record of this period. It is especially valuable for deaths in the 1870s-1880s.

- **Use triennial tax assessments as census substitutes.** Pennsylvania assessed coal-region residents every three years from 1853, per [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records). The ledgers note occupation and sometimes nativity — useful for locating a miner between decennial censuses and for filling the destroyed 1890 gap.

- **The 1880 census is the most important single census for this window.** It is the first to record household relationships. Per [Pennsylvania Genealogy, Census Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania,_United_States_Genealogy#Census_Records), cross-referencing the 1870 and 1880 censuses together establishes family composition on both sides of the 1878 Lackawanna/Luzerne split.

- **Distinguish payroll indexes from accident reports.** Per [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records), payroll-derived indexes are organized by individual worker name; mine-inspection and accident reports are by colliery. Use payroll indexes for a person-level search first. Accident reports are still genealogically valuable — they name the deceased and witnesses, and may record the only dated event tying a man to a specific colliery.

- **Schuylkill County church records (imageGroupNumber 007936751) contain both English and German entries.** The volume (1842-1895, 187 images) is browse-only with no name index. German-language entries will require reading the original language.

- **Consider DNA evidence** as a complement to documentary research. Irish coal-region families often emigrated in community waves from the same townland; DNA matching on GEDmatch or MyHeritage may identify cousins from the same origin community whose trees supply the Irish parish and parents you cannot yet document.

# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region (1860–1890)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Counties covered:** Schuylkill (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton), Luzerne (formed 1786), Lackawanna (formed 1878 from Luzerne), Carbon (formed 1843 from Monroe and Northampton), Northumberland (formed 1772)
- **County seats:** Pottsville (Schuylkill), Wilkes-Barre (Luzerne), Scranton (Lackawanna), Jim Thorpe / Mauch Chunk (Carbon), Sunbury (Northumberland)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period (Schuylkill County, as anchor):** 89,510 (1860) → 116,428 (1870) → 129,974 (1880); Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, and Northumberland show comparable rapid growth driven by coal.
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining dominated all five counties; collieries, breaker operations, company towns, canal and railroad transport of coal.
- **Ethnic composition:** Large Irish immigrant population (especially post-Famine 1845-1855 arrivals working through the 1860s-1890s); Welsh miners; German settlers; smaller Eastern European presence growing by the 1880s.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant among Irish, with parishes founded 1840-1870); Welsh Calvinist Methodist; Presbyterian; Lutheran; German Reformed; Episcopal.
- **Key historical events:** Molly Maguires trial and executions (1877, Schuylkill County); Long Strike of 1875; formation of Lackawanna County from Luzerne (1878); growth of the Philadelphia and Reading Railroad; Mine Safety Act (1869 Pennsylvania).

## Boundary changes
- **Lackawanna County formed 1878 from Luzerne County.** All records for the Scranton/Carbondale/Carbondale area before 1878 are held under Luzerne County — search Luzerne for any event there before that year.
- **Schuylkill County formed 1811** from Berks and Northampton; no relevant boundary changes within the 1860-1890 window.
- **Carbon County formed 1843** from Monroe and Northampton; stable through the target period.
- **Northumberland County formed 1772;** oldest of the five; stable boundaries.
- **Luzerne County formed 1786;** lost its northern section to form Lackawanna in 1878.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania statewide civil registration of births and deaths did not begin until **1906** at the state level. The entire 1860-1890 target window falls before any statewide requirement. County-level registration was not mandated during this period. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania Vital Records, Civil Registration, and related sub-pages returned only generic content in this survey — no Pennsylvania-specific start dates were returned by the tool.
- **What exists (state-level collections found):** Pennsylvania Death Certificates, 1906-1968 (FamilySearch collection 2255317, 4,218,763 indexed records with images) — this is entirely post-period. Pennsylvania County Marriages, 1885-1950 (collection 1921317, 524,189 indexed records, 312,045 images) — the 1885-1890 slice partially overlaps the target window. Pennsylvania Civil Marriages, 1677-1950 (collection 1571957, 312,045 indexed records) and Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages, 1700-1900 (collection 1502909, 198,765 indexed records, no images) both cover the period.
- **For the 1860-1890 window specifically:** Church registers are the primary birth and death sources. Marriage records at the county courthouse (Recorder of Deeds / Orphans' Court) exist but are largely unindexed in digital form for this period.
- **Schuylkill County marriage volumes digitized:** FamilySearch imageGroupNumber 007936753, covering 1870-1910, 94 images — browse-only (0% indexed, not full-text searchable).
- **Gaps:** No statewide birth or death registration during 1860-1890. Pre-registration alternatives are church records (see below).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (most Irish parishes); Welsh Calvinist Methodist; Presbyterian; Lutheran; German Reformed; Episcopal.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, and confirmations. Catholic registers also include First Communion and parish census (status animarum) books.
- **Where held:**
  - Diocese of Scranton (formed 1868): holds records for most Lackawanna and northern Luzerne County parishes from 1868 forward. Contact: Diocese of Scranton Archives, 300 Wyoming Avenue, Scranton, PA 18503.
  - Diocese of Harrisburg: holds records for southern anthracite counties (Schuylkill, Carbon, Northumberland) and for all coal-region parishes before the Diocese of Scranton was carved out in 1868.
  - Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records), many Catholic parishes in the coal region were established between 1840 and 1870 specifically to serve Irish and Eastern European immigrant communities; baptismal registers for these parishes are the primary Irish-ancestry vital evidence for 1860-1890.
  - FamilySearch digitized Schuylkill County church records (imageGroupNumber 007936751, 1842-1895, 187 images, languages: English and German) — browse-only images, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable. Must be examined image by image. Note: German-language entries require reading the original language.
- **Language:** English and German; Latin used in formal Catholic sacramental entries.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Pennsylvania is covered in all federal censuses. Relevant years: 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900. Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania,_United_States_Genealogy#Census_Records): the 1880 census is the first to record household relationships — especially valuable for proving family connections. The 1870 and 1900 censuses bracket the 1890 destruction gap. The 1890 population schedules are almost entirely destroyed nationwide.
- **Mortality schedules:** The federal mortality schedules (1850-1885) record deaths in the year preceding each census — relevant for 1860, 1870, and 1880 enumerations.
- **State/other enumerations:** Pennsylvania triennial tax assessments (from 1853) serve as intercensal substitutes; see Tax Records below.
- **Access:** The 1860, 1870, 1880, and 1900 federal censuses are fully indexed and available on FamilySearch (free) and Ancestry (subscription). FamilySearch externally curated: 1850 United States Federal Census - Schuylkill County on Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/1276/).

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills (testate estates), letters of administration (intestate estates), guardianship petitions for minor children, inventories, estate distributions. For an Irish miner who died without a will — common — look for the administration file, not the will index.
- **Date range:** From county formation through the period.
- **Where held (county level):** Register of Wills at each county courthouse. Schuylkill County probate records are digitized on FamilySearch: imageGroupNumber 007936749, covering 1851-1930, 412 images — browse-only (0% indexed, not full-text searchable). Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994 (FamilySearch collection 1999196, 3,200,560 images, 0 indexed records) — images present but not name-searchable.
- **Naturalization records (court-held):** Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Naturalization_Records), pre-1906 naturalizations are scattered across Quarter Sessions, Common Pleas, and Orphans' Courts in each county. Declarations of intent and petitions for naturalization name the applicant's country of origin — critical for tracing Irish origins. Schuylkill County naturalization records are digitized: imageGroupNumber 007936750, 1849-1915, 298 images — browse-only (0% indexed). After September 1906, NARA Philadelphia holds federal court naturalizations for eastern Pennsylvania.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is a state-land state).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The Pennsylvania Land Office (Commonwealth of Pennsylvania) issued warrants and patents; the county Recorder of Deeds holds deed transfers. FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania Land and Property returned only generic content in this survey.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, sheriff's deeds, tax records. Company-owned colliery housing means many miners did not hold land in their own name — sheriff's sales and mortgage records may be more relevant than straightforward deeds.
- **Where held:** County Recorder of Deeds. Schuylkill County deed records digitized on FamilySearch: imageGroupNumber 007936752, 1815-1900, 543 images, 22% name-indexed (partial name search possible, but most images must be browsed). This is the only partially indexed Schuylkill volume found in this survey.
- **Tax records:** Pennsylvania state assessors enumerated coal-region residents triennially from 1853 (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records). Ledgers list householder, real estate value, occupation, and sometimes nativity. These triennial assessments (1853, 1856, 1859, 1862, 1865, 1868, 1871, 1874, 1877, 1880, 1883, 1886, 1889) serve as census substitutes and occupation verifiers for coal miners.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861-1865). Many Irish anthracite miners served in Pennsylvania volunteer regiments.
- **Record types:** Service records and pension files at NARA; Pennsylvania Civil War Muster Rolls at the Pennsylvania State Archives; pension files (which include age, birthplace, and family information) available on Fold3 and Ancestry.
- **Where held:** NARA (National Personnel Records Center / NARA Washington for Civil War service and pension records); Pennsylvania State Archives, 350 North Street, Harrisburg, PA 17120.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Catholic parish cemeteries in each coal town (most attached to Irish-founded parishes); non-sectarian borough cemeteries; company-owned cemeteries at some collieries.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) and BillionGraves index many coal-region headstones but coverage is incomplete — physical visits may be needed for smaller parish cemeteries.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records at individual parishes or borough offices; Catholic parish burial registers held by diocesan archives (see Church Records above).

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Miners' Journal (Pottsville, Schuylkill County, 1825-present) is the most important — it covered the entire anthracite region, published obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices, and trial coverage (including Molly Maguire proceedings). Scranton Republican, Wilkes-Barre Record, and Carbon Advocate are relevant for northern counties.
- **Where held:** Miners' Journal historical issues are available on microfilm at the Schuylkill County Historical Society and partially digitized. Check Chronicling America (Library of Congress) for partially digitized Pennsylvania newspapers.
- **Content value:** Obituaries frequently name the deceased's county of origin in Ireland, spouse, and surviving children — extremely high value for Irish immigrant research.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia (primary arrival port for Irish immigrants to eastern Pennsylvania); New York (Castle Garden 1855-1890, Ellis Island from 1892); Baltimore.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists at NARA and Ancestry; naturalization declarations (county courts, pre-1906); border crossing records; passport applications.
- **Where held:** NARA Mid-Atlantic Region (Philadelphia) for Philadelphia port records; NARA New York for New York arrivals; both are digitized on Ancestry and FamilySearch.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard including infants and young children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest for all family members when researching a family arrival. Post-1895 lists include place of last residence and contact person in the destination country.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Pennsylvania triennial state property assessment ledgers (from 1853); county poor tax; personal property tax.
- **Date range:** Triennial from 1853 onward through the target window.
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives and individual county courthouses / historical societies.
- **Substitute value:** Triennial assessments at regular three-year intervals serve as intercensal evidence between the 1860, 1870, 1880 federal censuses and substitute for the destroyed 1890 census. They also verify occupation as 'miner' or a specific colliery role.

### Specialized coal-region indexes
- **Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855-1898:** Per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records, this index names approximately 41,000 colliery workers across the anthracite field, drawn from company payroll books that survived a 1903 records consolidation. Entries include occupation (loader, breaker boy, mule driver), wage rate, and parish of origin where stated. This is the most direct finding aid for Irish immigrant miners in the northern anthracite counties (Lackawanna, Luzerne) whose names were indexed inconsistently in census records.
- **Company payroll indexes vs. mine-inspection reports:** Per the same FamilySearch Wiki page, payroll-derived indexes name individual workers; mine-inspection and accident reports are organized by colliery, not by person. Use the payroll index first for a named individual. Accident reports are still valuable — they name the deceased and witnesses.

### Other record types
- **Occupational records:** Mine inspection reports (organized by colliery); coal company employment records where they survive; union records (Workingmen's Benevolent Association, 1868-1875; United Mine Workers of America from 1890).
- **Institutional records:** Miners' hospital and dispensary records; almshouse records at county level (for destitute miners or widows).
- **Town and county histories:** 19th-century published local histories for Schuylkill, Luzerne, and Carbon counties frequently contain biographical sketches of prominent residents and reprint early records. Available through WorldCat and the FamilySearch Catalog.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Schuylkill Co. Church Records (1708-1985, collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, 607,220 images); Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683-1994 (collection 1999196, 3.2M images, browse-only); Pennsylvania County Marriages 1885-1950 (collection 1921317, 524,189 indexed records); Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677-1950 (collection 1571957, 312,045 indexed records); Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages 1700-1900 (collection 1502909, 198,765 indexed records, no images); Schuylkill Co. deed volumes, naturalization volumes, church volumes, probate volumes, and marriage volumes (5 digitized volumes, imageGroupNumbers 007936749-007936753, all browse-only except deeds at 22% indexed) | Free |
| Ancestry | Pennsylvania Tax and Exoneration Lists 1768-1801; 1850 US Federal Census - Schuylkill County; federal censuses 1860-1900; Civil War pension files (Fold3); passenger lists | Subscription |
| Chronicling America (LOC) | Partial digitization of Pennsylvania newspapers including Miners' Journal | Free |
| Fold3 | Civil War service records and pension files | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** 5 digitized volumes match Schuylkill County for the 1860-1890 period; this was the complete result set (totalResults: 5, no nextPageToken). Only Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, and Northumberland county volumes were not separately retrieved — a coverage gap in this survey for those counties.

### Physical repositories

| Diocese of Harrisburg Archives | Catholic parish registers for southern anthracite counties; all coal-region parishes pre-1868 | Write or call for access |
| NARA Mid-Atlantic Region, Philadelphia | Philadelphia port passenger arrivals; post-1906 federal naturalization records | In-person or Ancestry/FamilySearch |
| County courthouses (Pottsville, Wilkes-Barre, Scranton, Jim Thorpe, Sunbury) | Original deed books, naturalization files, probate files, marriage licenses | In-person or mail request |
| Luzerne County Historical Society | Records covering the entire pre-1878 region including what is now Lackawanna County | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- Triennial state tax assessment ledgers for most years (physical at Pennsylvania State Archives and county repositories)
- Pre-1906 naturalization petitions for Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, and Northumberland counties (not yet digitized in FamilySearch as of this survey; Schuylkill volumes are digitized but browse-only)
- Most Catholic parish baptismal and burial registers (held at diocesan archives, not publicly digitized)

Here is the locality guide the agent produced:

---

## Vermont Pre-Statehood Locality Research Guide

### The Core Challenge: Three Competing Jurisdictions

Vermont in the late 1700s is genealogically unique because the same land was simultaneously claimed and recorded by **three different authorities**:

1. **New Hampshire** — issued the original "New Hampshire Grants" town charters beginning in the 1740s–1760s under Governor Benning Wentworth
2. **New York** — refused to recognize those grants and attempted to re-grant the same land under its own authority
3. **The Vermont Republic (1777–1791)** — declared independence from both and began keeping its own records

An ancestor's land transaction may appear in records held today in **Concord, Albany, or Montpelier** — possibly all three. This overlap is the single most important structural fact for researching this period.

---

### Jurisdictional Timeline

| Period | Authority | Where Records Are Held |
|---|---|---|
| ~1749–1777 | New Hampshire Grants | New Hampshire State Archives, Concord |
| ~1764–1777 | New York counter-claims | New York State Archives, Albany |
| 1777–1791 | Vermont Republic | Vermont State Archives, Montpelier |
| 1791–present | State of Vermont | Vermont State Archives + town clerks |

---

### Record Types and What Survives

#### Vital Records (Births, Marriages, Deaths)
- Vermont had **no statewide vital registration before 1857**. For the pre-statehood period, you must go to:
  - **Town clerk records** — surviving unevenly from the 1770s onward; quality varies town to town
  - **Church registers** — Congregational, Baptist, and Quaker congregations kept registers; survival is uneven
  - **Gravestone inscriptions** — transcribed by the Daughters of the American Revolution and the Vermont Old Cemetery Association

#### Land and Property
- **New Hampshire Grants / Proprietors' Records**: The 1771 survey listed approximately 1,800 land grantees by name — a valuable name index for the pre-revolutionary period
- **New York Patents**: If your ancestor's land was disputed, look for counter-grant records in Albany
- **Vermont Republic Land Records**: Town-level deed books begin in many towns in the late 1770s–1780s
- The **Vermont State Papers** (published multi-volume set) include many pre-statehood land documents in print

#### Census and Tax Records
- **1790 Federal Census** — Vermont's first federal census; covers all of the state and is fully indexed. This is the primary starting point for working backward into the pre-statehood years.
- **Grand Lists (Tax Lists)** — Towns assessed taxable property annually. Many survive from the 1780s and serve as substitutes for missing vital and census records. Held at the town level and at the Vermont State Archives.

#### Church Records
- Congregational churches (the dominant denomination) kept registers of baptisms, marriages, and burials; survival is uneven
- Some Presbyterian, Baptist, and Quaker records survive and have been published or microfilmed
- FamilySearch has microfilmed a substantial portion of Vermont church records

#### Probate Records
- Vermont probate courts were organized by county beginning in 1778
- Probate records for the pre-statehood period are held at the **county probate district offices** and copies are at the Vermont State Archives
- FamilySearch has microfilmed most pre-1900 probate files

#### Military Records
- Vermont men served in the American Revolution. Look for:
  - **Vermont Revolutionary War pension files** at the National Archives (NARA)
  - **Vermont in the Revolution** (published roster of soldiers)
  - **Bounty land warrant applications** — NARA, often name-indexed

---

### Key Repositories

| Repository | What It Holds |
|---|---|
| **Vermont State Archives, Montpelier** | Republic-era and state land records, legislative papers, early court records |
| **Vermont town clerks** | Vital records, land deeds, grand lists — held at the individual town level |
| **New Hampshire Division of Archives and Records Management, Concord** | New Hampshire Grants, Wentworth charters |
| **New York State Archives, Albany** | New York counter-grants, Adirondack/Champlain patent records |
| **National Archives (NARA)** | Revolutionary War pension files, bounty land warrants, 1790 census |
| **Vermont Historical Society, Barre** | Published town histories, diaries, newspapers, genealogical collections |
| **FamilySearch (online & microfilm)** | Substantial digitized and microfilmed coverage of Vermont vital records, probate, church records, and censuses |

---

### FamilySearch Resources for Vermont

The FamilySearch Wiki's Vermont Genealogy page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy) documents the following collections and starting points:

- **FamilySearch Catalog** — Search by "Vermont" and then by county or town to find specific microfilmed record sets (probate, church, land, vital records)
- Digitized Vermont records are browsable and searchable through FamilySearch's main record search
- Many Vermont town vital records (even pre-1857 entries recorded retrospectively) have been indexed

**Recommended FamilySearch search path:**
1. Start with the **1790 U.S. Federal Census** (indexed, fully searchable)
2. Search **Vermont Vital Records 1760–1954** (a compiled statewide index)
3. Search **Vermont Probate Records** by county
4. Use the **FamilySearch Catalog** to identify microfilmed town-clerk and church record volumes for your specific town

---

### Recommended Research Sequence for Pre-Statehood Vermont

1. **1790 Federal Census** — Locate the household; note county and town
2. **Grand Lists (tax records)** for the 1780s — Confirm presence and track backward
3. **Town clerk vital records** — Check what your specific town preserved
4. **Church registers** — Identify the congregation and search its register
5. **Probate records** — Search county probate district for wills and inventories
6. **Land records** — Town deed books, then New Hampshire Grants if pre-1777
7. **New York land records** — If the town was in a disputed grant area (much of western Vermont)
8. **Revolutionary War records** — NARA pension files and Vermont published rosters
9. **Published town histories** — Many Vermont towns produced 19th-century histories with genealogical appendices

---

### Important Reference Works

- *Vermont State Papers* (multi-volume, published) — includes many original Republic-era documents
- *Vermont in the Revolution* — roster of soldiers
- Hemenway's *Vermont Gazetteer* — town-by-town histories with genealogical data
- Daughters of the American Revolution cemetery transcriptions for Vermont

---

**Next step:** The agent notes that the best way to move forward is to build a research plan sequenced around your specific ancestor — starting with the 1790 census and working backward through tax lists, church registers, and proprietors' records. If you share the ancestor's name and the town or county they lived in, that plan can be built out in detail.

jurisdictions.name: Province of New Hampshire (New Hampshire Grants)

quirks: Statewide civil registration of births, marriages, and deaths did not begin until 1857 (statewide level). Town clerk records from the 1770s onward survive unevenly — contact each town clerk directly. No civil vital records existed before the Vermont Republic period.

The Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule (prepared under New York colonial authority) enumerates approximately 1,800 New Hampshire grant grantees with name, township, acreage, and disputed-claim status — it is the earliest systematic resident list for the future state, per the FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki page.

Any land transaction before 1777 may have a parallel record in both New Hampshire (original Wentworth grants, held at the NH Division of Archives) and New York (competing re-grants, held at the NY State Archives). Search both before concluding a deed does not exist.

19th-century Vermont town histories (most published 1860-1900) often reprint colonial-era proprietors' records otherwise difficult to access — they are essential sources, not merely supplementary, per the FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki page.

Families along the Connecticut River border may have records in New Hampshire (Cheshire/Sullivan counties); families along the western Lake Champlain shore may have records in New York (Clinton/Essex counties); families along the southern border may have records in Massachusetts (Franklin/Berkshire counties). Search all adjoining jurisdictions.
The 1790 federal census is the first systematic population count for Vermont. Tax grand lists from 1779 onward are the primary substitute for census coverage between 1777 and 1790.
Church registers for this period are largely not digitized or name-indexed; most must be ordered on microfilm through the Family History Library and browsed image by image.
No catastrophic statewide record loss has been identified, but individual town record survival is uneven; some towns' earliest records were lost to fire or damp storage.
